nameStory: The Savannah Monitor gets its name from the African grasslands and savannahs where it naturally roams. These wide-open landscapes of scattered trees and grasslands are its true home, though this particular lizard has found itself far from those sunny African plains. In Europe, it's called "Bosc's monitor" after French scientist Louis Bosc, who first described this impressive reptile to science.
description: The Savannah Monitor is a stocky, powerful lizard that can grow quite large - typically 3 to 4 feet long when fully grown. It has a thick, muscular body covered in small, bead-like scales that create an intricate pattern of light and dark bands across its back and tail. Its head is broad and triangular with a long, forked tongue that flicks out constantly to "taste" the air. This is definitely not a native New England reptile - it's an African species that occasionally turns up as an escaped or released pet.

idTips.label: Scales
idTips.description: Small, round, bead-like scales cover the entire body, feeling almost like tiny bumps under your finger. The scales have a slightly rough, pebbly texture unlike the smooth or keeled scales of native lizards.

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Bold crossbands of tan, brown, and darker brown create a striking striped pattern across the back and tail. The bands are crisp and well-defined, not blotchy or faded.

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Broad, triangular head that's noticeably wider than the neck, with small, alert eyes and external ear openings visible as dark holes behind the eyes.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Much larger than any native New England lizard - adults are typically 3-4 feet long with a thick, heavy build that makes them unmistakable.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Constantly flicks its long, deeply forked tongue to sample scents in the air. Moves with a confident, almost swaggering gait unlike the quick, darting movements of native lizards.

habitat: This species has no natural habitat in New England - any sighting would be an escaped or abandoned pet. If encountered, it would likely be found near human habitation, possibly seeking warmth around buildings, compost piles, or sunny, sheltered areas. An escaped monitor might temporarily survive in rocky areas or woodland edges during warm weather.

seasonality.spring: Any sighting would likely be of a recently escaped pet as temperatures warm enough for reptile activity. Would be sluggish and seeking warm, sunny spots.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for sightings as escaped pets could temporarily survive outdoors. Would be most active during warm days, basking in sunny areas.
seasonality.fall: Extremely unlikely to survive cooling temperatures. Any escaped individual would become increasingly sluggish and seek shelter.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors. Any previous escapees would have succumbed to cold temperatures or been recaptured.

funFact: Savannah Monitors are accomplished diggers that create burrows up to 6 feet deep in their African homeland, and they're surprisingly good swimmers despite their chunky appearance - they can hold their breath underwater for over an hour!
confusionNotes: Unlikely to be confused with any native New England reptile due to its large size and distinctive banded pattern. The only similar-looking animals would be other escaped monitor lizards or large constrictors, but the small, beaded scales and forked tongue are unmistakable.
contextualKnowledge: This is a popular pet reptile that requires specialized care and can live 15-20 years. Many are abandoned or escape when owners realize how large and demanding they become. If encountered, contact local animal control - these are not dangerous to humans but need proper care and cannot survive New England winters.
compareHints: As the only monitor lizard species recorded in New England, it's unmistakable among its genus. Compared to other large reptiles that might be kept as pets, monitors have distinctively small, bead-like scales rather than the large, overlapping scales of iguanas or the smooth skin of tegus. The constantly flicking forked tongue and powerful build make identification straightforward.
